name: Aramaic
blurb: Aramaic is written from right to left in 22 letters, all consonants, like Hebrew and Phoenician; its alphabet spread across the Persian empire and gave rise to the Hebrew, Syriac, Nabataean and Arabic scripts.

scripts.label: Imperial Aramaic
scripts.about: The letters of the Persian chancery (6th–4th centuries BCE), used for letters and contracts from Egypt to Afghanistan, as in the papyri of Elephantine.
scripts.note: Type as it sounds: sh for š, ch for ḥ, ts for ṣ, ' for aleph and ` for ʿayin. Short vowels inside a word are left out; i becomes י-like yodh and o or u waw; a final a is written with aleph, as in malka, mlkʾ, “the king”.
groups: aleph · a catch in the throat; also a final a
waw · w; also o and u
ʿayin · a sound squeezed in the throat
qoph · k, said deep in the throat
samples: “Mene, mene, tekel, upharsin”: the writing on the wall at Belshazzar’s feast

scripts.label: Syriac (Estrangela)
scripts.about: The script of Syriac, the Aramaic of Edessa and of the Christians of Mesopotamia, in Estrangela, its oldest book hand (from the 1st century CE); the letters join like Arabic.
scripts.note: The same 22 letters, joined in Syriac fashion. Type as for Imperial Aramaic: sh, ch, ts, ' for alaph and ` for ʿe. Short vowels inside a word are left out; a final a takes alaph, as in shlama, ܫܠܡܐ.
groups: alaph · a catch in the throat; also a final a
waw · w; also o and u
ʿe · a sound squeezed in the throat
qaph · k, said deep in the throat
samples: “Our Father, who art in heaven”: the Lord’s Prayer in the Syriac Bible
